standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: @RequestBody is what turns incoming JSON bytes into a Java object you can work with — one annotation does the whole job.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RequestBody tells Spring to read the HTTP request body and deserialize it into the annotated Java parameter. Jackson's ObjectMapper does the actual work — it reads the JSON and populates your Java object's fields.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Without @RequestBody, you'd have to manually read the request input stream and parse JSON yourself. With it, you just declare the type you want and Spring delivers a populated object.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: The client must send Content-Type: application/json — without it, Spring returns 415 Unsupported Media Type.
Add @Valid before @RequestBody to trigger Bean Validation automatically on the deserialized object.
If validation fails, Spring returns 400 Bad Request without your method body ever running.
required=false makes the body optional — useful when the body might be absent.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: sharp edge: If Jackson can't parse the incoming JSON to the target type — wrong field name, wrong type — it throws HttpMessageNotReadableException and returns 400. The error message tells you exactly which field failed, but only if you log it. In production, many teams swallow this into a generic error response and lose the detail.

cap: The @Valid + @RequestBody combination is the standard pattern for POST and PUT endpoints — it handles both deserialization and validation in one shot.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: @ResponseBody flips the direction — instead of going to a template, your return value goes straight to the response as JSON.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @ResponseBody tells Spring that a method's return value should be written directly into the HTTP response body, not treated as a view name. Jackson serializes the return object to JSON and Spring sets Content-Type to application/json.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: In a traditional @Controller, return values are view names — Spring looks for a template file. @ResponseBody overrides that behavior for specific methods. @RestController puts @ResponseBody on every method in the class implicitly.

beats.label: example
beats.content: The only time you'd add @ResponseBody explicitly is in a @Controller class that mostly returns HTML pages, but needs one specific method to return JSON. You're mixing view-based and REST endpoints in the same class.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: candidates miss: If a @RestController method returns null, Spring writes an empty body with status 200 — not a 404. If a method returns void, same thing: 200 with no body. Returning null is rarely the right behavior; use ResponseEntity.notFound() or throw a proper exception instead.

cap: @RequestBody and @ResponseBody are mirrors: one deserializes incoming JSON, the other serializes outgoing objects. Together they define the contract of your REST endpoint.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Adding @Valid before @RequestBody turns your controller into a validator — no if-null checks, no boilerplate.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: When you add @Valid before @RequestBody, Spring runs Bean Validation on the deserialized object before your method body runs. If any constraint fails, Spring automatically returns 400 Bad Request with error details.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: You annotate your DTO fields with validation constraints. @NotBlank for required strings, @Email for email format, @Min and @Max for number ranges, @Size for length. When the request comes in, Spring checks all of them in one pass.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: @NotBlank: string must not be null, empty, or whitespace.
@Email: string must be a valid email format.
@Min and @Max: number must be within the given range.
@Size(min, max): string or collection must be within the length range.
@Pattern(regexp): string must match a custom regular expression.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: non-obvious: The default 400 response from Spring is a MethodArgumentNotValidException with a nested error structure. Most production teams add a @ControllerAdvice to catch this exception and return a clean, consistent error JSON — like a list of field names and their error messages. Without that, the default error body can be verbose and inconsistent.

cap: Add spring-boot-starter-validation to your pom.xml or build.gradle — without it, the @Valid annotation is present but the constraints are silently ignored.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: @RequestHeader saves you from digging into HttpServletRequest just to read one header value.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: @RequestHeader extracts a specific HTTP request header into a method parameter. @CookieValue does the same for cookie values. Spring binds them by name automatically.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: The alternative is injecting HttpServletRequest and calling getHeader manually. @RequestHeader is cleaner, testable, and declarative — the method signature documents exactly which headers the endpoint depends on.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: required=false with defaultValue: makes the header optional and provides a fallback.
Map<String, String> with @RequestHeader: injects all headers at once.
HTTP headers are case-insensitive — Spring normalizes casing automatically.
@CookieValue follows the same pattern for cookie names.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: gotcha: If a required header is missing, Spring returns 400 Bad Request with a MissingRequestHeaderException. If you expect the header might not always be present — like an optional correlation ID — mark it required=false so missing headers don't break the request.

cap: Common real-world use: extract the Authorization Bearer token from the Authorization header for manual validation before Spring Security is in place.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: @RequestParam and @RequestBody both get data from the client — but from completely different places.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @RequestParam reads from the URL query string — those key-value pairs after the question mark. Something like /users?page=0&size=10&status=ACTIVE. Simple primitive types and strings.

beats.label: what_each_is
beats.content: @RequestBody reads from the HTTP request body — typically a JSON payload. Used for complex objects in POST and PUT requests. The client sends JSON, Jackson deserializes it into your Java object.

beats.label: when_to_pick
beats.content: Use @RequestParam for filtering, sorting, and pagination parameters in GET requests. Use @RequestBody for the main payload in create and update operations. You can use both in the same method — for example, a POST with a JSON body and a ?dryRun=true query parameter.

beats.label: tiny_example
beats.content: candidates miss: GET requests technically can have a body, but it's against REST conventions and many proxies and clients strip it. Never use @RequestBody on a GET endpoint in practice.

cap: A simple rule: GET requests use @RequestParam and @PathVariable. POST and PUT requests use @RequestBody for the main data.

standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API serving a mobile client
hook: Returning your JPA entity directly from a REST controller works — until it causes a security leak or a serialization crash.

beats.label: what_it_is
beats.content: A DTO — Data Transfer Object — is a plain Java class designed specifically for API input or output. It contains only the fields the API needs, nothing more. You map between your entity and DTO explicitly.

beats.label: why_it_exists
beats.content: Your JPA entity maps to your database schema. Your API contract is a different concern. Tying them together means a column rename in the database breaks your API, and adding an internal field to the entity exposes it in every response.

beats.label: parts_or_states
content: Security: a User entity might have a passwordHash field. A DTO exposes only name and email.
Lazy loading: Jackson serializes entity fields eagerly. Lazy collections hit the database after the transaction closes, causing LazyInitializationException.
Circular references: bidirectional JPA relationships cause infinite recursion during serialization.
Decoupling: rename a database column without changing your API contract.

beats.label: pitfalls
beats.content: production trap: The LazyInitializationException and infinite recursion bugs from returning entities directly are the two most common Jackson errors in fresher codebases. Interviewers know this and ask about it to filter candidates who've only done toy projects.

cap: Use separate request and response DTOs. MapStruct generates the mapping code at compile time with zero reflection overhead.
